memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: All these latter kings joined forces in the Valley of Siddim (that is, the Dead Sea Valley). For twelve years they had been subject to Kedorlaomer, but in the thirteenth year they rebelled. - Gen 14:3-4 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Twelve years of submission, and then rebellion. The kings of the plain had been paying tribute to a stronger power, and finally they had enough. They threw off the yoke - and, as we'll see, it went badly for them. Their rebellion brought armies down on their heads.

This is how the world's power works: strength dominates until a stronger strength overturns it, and round it goes. There is no justice in it, only force. The nations of the Dead Sea Valley weren't fighting for righteousness; they simply wanted out from under someone else's boot.

Notice that Scripture reports this without approval or condemnation. It simply tells us what happened. Human politics grinds on - alliances, tribute, revolt, retaliation - and God's story moves through the middle of it.

Yet the Bible does have something to say about rebellion in a deeper sense. Every human heart, left to itself, wants to throw off God's rule. "We all, like sheep, have gone astray, each of us has turned to our own way" (Isa 53:6). The difference is that God's rule is not tyranny to escape but goodness to enjoy. The kings rebelled against a cruel overlord and were crushed. We rebel against a loving Father - and He sent His Son to bring us home.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
- Where do you resist God's rule, treating it as a burden rather than a blessing?
- How is God's authority different from every human power?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text:
Father, forgive the rebellion in my heart that wants my own way. Thank You that Your rule is not tyranny but love. Teach me to gladly live under Your good authority.
Amen.
